planting.note: Plant container stock in spring in well-drained soil in full sun; this New Zealand native briefly drops its tiny rounded leaflets in late winter just before a flush of pendulous golden-yellow pea flowers opens on bare branches.

directions: Set out young plants in a sheltered, sunny spot with sharp drainage, since kowhai resents soggy winter soil. Expect an open, slightly weeping branch structure that can be trained as a single-trunk specimen or espalier against a warm wall. The spring flower flush is a magnet for nectar-feeding birds in mild climates, and seed pods that follow are winged and papery. Water regularly while young but taper off once established, as mature trees are quite drought tolerant.

planting.note: Plant in spring in gritty, sharply drained soil in full sun, mimicking the rocky coastal cliffs of its native Cook Strait habitat.

directions: This compact, naturally dwarf kowhai cultivar stays shrubby rather than tree-like, making it useful for smaller gardens, coastal plantings, or large containers. Deep golden-yellow flowers cluster along the branches in late winter and early spring, well before most other shrubs bloom. Prune lightly after flowering to maintain a dense habit, and avoid heavy, wet soils that encourage root rot. It tolerates wind and salt spray far better than the larger tree kowhai species.

planting.note: Plant container stock in spring in lean, very well-drained, low-phosphorus soil in full sun; this classic hybrid dislikes rich garden fertilizers.

directions: One of the most widely planted grevillea hybrids, this cultivar produces curved, toothbrush-shaped red-and-pink flower clusters almost continuously from spring through fall, drawing honeyeaters and hummingbirds alike. It forms a dense, rounded mound of narrow, divided green foliage and tolerates poor, sandy soils as long as drainage is sharp. Avoid phosphorus-rich fertilizers, which can injure the roots of many Australian proteaceous shrubs. Light tip-pruning after flushes of bloom keeps growth compact and encourages repeat flowering.

planting.note: Plant in spring on a sunny slope or bank in gritty, fast-draining soil; this trailing cultivar is prized for holding embankments and spilling over retaining walls.

directions: Part of the famous Poorinda series of Grevillea hybrids bred in Victoria, this selection stays low and ground-hugging while spreading widely, rooting as it creeps along the soil surface. Deep red, spidery flower clusters appear mostly in cooler months and attract nectar-feeding birds. It is an excellent erosion-control planting on dry banks where little else will thrive, and needs no fertilizing beyond an occasional low-phosphorus native blend. Trim back any overly long runners to keep the mat tidy near paths or walls.

planting.note: Plant in spring in lean, acidic, sharply drained soil in full sun; this fynbos hybrid needs the same low-phosphorus regime as its protea relatives.

directions: Grown chiefly for its glowing golden-yellow bracts that surround small central cones through winter and spring, this hybrid is a mainstay of the cut-flower trade from Cape fynbos nurseries. It wants lean, acidic, mineral soil with excellent drainage and resents both rich compost and standing moisture around the roots. Cutting stems for arrangements doubles as a pruning that keeps the shrub shapely and encourages fresh colorful growth. Protect from hard frost and from phosphorus fertilizers, which can quickly kill fynbos shrubs.

planting.note: Plant in spring or fall in average, well-drained soil in full sun to light shade; its narrow columnar habit fits tight spaces where the invasive wild species would never be used.

directions: This sterile, non-fruiting selection was bred specifically to give gardeners the fine, fern-like, deeply dissected foliage of common buckthorn without the seedy reseeding that has made the wild species invasive across the northern United States and Canada. Its tight, upright, columnar form makes it useful as a narrow privacy screen, hedge accent, or foundation planting where width is limited. Foliage turns soft yellow in fall, and the plant tolerates a wide range of soils including clay and urban conditions. Little pruning is needed to maintain its naturally narrow shape.
